The South America Guide: Six Regions Beyond the Marquee Images

Argentina, Chile, Peru, the Galápagos, Colombia, and Brazil — why the continent's luxury travel product is underused almost entirely because of a perception gap that stopped reflecting reality years ago, and the six regions worth understanding before it does.

Home›Travel Journal›Destination Guide›South America
MS
Mark Sole Founder & Travel Director, Hit Your Mark Travel
Share

South America is the continent that travel writing has never quite captured accurately. The marquee images most travelers carry — Machu Picchu at dawn, the granite towers of Patagonia, Carnaval in Rio — are all real and all correct, but they represent a fraction of what the continent actually delivers at the luxury end of the market, and their familiarity has created a perception of the region as a set of two or three known quantities rather than a continent of genuine breadth. The Atacama Desert in northern Chile is the driest non-polar desert on earth — a moonscape of salt flats, geysers, and flamingo lagoons at 2,400 meters altitude — and has a small-lodge hospitality scene built specifically around its landscape that rivals anything in Jordan or Namibia. Lima's food culture is, by the current assessment of critics who follow these things, the most exciting in the Western Hemisphere. The Pantanal wetland in Brazil produces jaguar sightings with a reliability that the Masai Mara produces lion sightings, and the Pantanal is largely unknown to the US traveler market. The continent's luxury travel product has matured significantly over the past fifteen years and is genuinely underused — almost entirely because of a perception lag that has not kept pace with the reality on the ground.

The planning challenge in South America is different from every other region in this series. The seasonal logic is inverted — the continent is in the Southern Hemisphere, which means Patagonia's summer runs November through March, the opposite of what travelers from the Northern Hemisphere are accustomed to planning around. More significantly, the continent's best destinations have seasonal windows that don't align with each other: the Inca Trail and Galápagos diving are best in the dry season (May–October); Patagonia and Mendoza wine harvest are best in the austral summer (November–April); the Pantanal jaguars concentrate in July–October; Lima and Cartagena are year-round. A multi-destination South America trip requires more seasonal coordination than any other continent in this guide series, and the itineraries that ignore this tend to deliver a diluted version of every destination on the list.

This guide covers six South American regions — Argentina, Chile, Peru, the Galápagos, Colombia, and Brazil — that each represent a fundamentally different travel experience and each have a specific seasonal window worth respecting.

The Hemisphere Logic

The single most common South America planning mistake made by travelers from the US and Europe is booking Patagonia in July because July is summer at home. July is winter in Patagonia. The park roads are partly closed, the weather is at its most extreme, and the famous Torres del Paine circuit is inaccessible in sections. The correct Patagonia window is November through March, peaking in December and January — when the days are long, the wildflowers are out, and the glaciers calve with enough frequency that you can time a visit to a viewpoint and watch it happen. If the itinerary also includes Peru's Inca Trail, which closes in February for maintenance and is best in May–October's dry season, the logical structure is to bookend: Galápagos and Peru in May–October, Patagonia and Argentina in November–March, with the shoulder months of April and November serving as the connecting tissue where both windows have partial overlap.

"The Galápagos is the only place on earth where the wildlife doesn't move when you approach — because nothing in its evolutionary history has ever given it a reason to. The encounter that results is unlike anything else in the natural world."

Six Regions at a Glance

Below is a breakdown of each region — its character, who it's right for, when to go, and the specific properties worth knowing. A timing guide and property reference section follow.

The Regions
Six Regions. Six Different South Americas.
01
Argentina — Buenos Aires, Patagonia & Mendoza
Best City Wilderness Wine
Buenos Aires · Torres del Paine · Perito Moreno · Fitz Roy · Mendoza · Iguazú
Argentina contains three separate travel experiences of the first order that share a country but almost nothing else. Buenos Aires is the most European city in the Americas — the Beaux-Arts architecture of the Recoleta neighborhood, the café culture, the late dinner at 10pm followed by tango at midnight, the steak-and-Malbec food tradition that operates with the seriousness of a French grand cuisine — and is consistently undervalued as a city destination by travelers who see it as a transit hub to Patagonia rather than a destination in itself. Three nights in Buenos Aires with the right restaurant reservations and a Saturday morning antiques market in San Telmo produces a trip that stands independently of anything further south.

Argentine Patagonia — Los Glaciares National Park, the Perito Moreno Glacier, the Fitz Roy massif at El Chaltén — is the southern hemisphere's finest wilderness destination for the non-Africa traveler. The Perito Moreno Glacier is 30 kilometers long, 5 kilometers wide, and advances continuously at a rate of two meters per day, calving chunks the size of buildings into the grey-blue Lago Argentino with a sound that registers as a geological event rather than a natural occurrence. Mendoza, in the Andes foothills at 800 meters altitude, produces the finest Malbec in the world and has built a winery and luxury lodge circuit in the Luján de Cuyo and Valle de Uco subregions that is the equal of any wine destination in this guide series.
Patagonia Best: November – March (austral summer; accessible trails; calving glacier) Mendoza Harvest: March – April (vendimia festival; best grape-to-wine timing) Buenos Aires: Year-round; March–May and September–November most pleasant Gateway: EZE (Buenos Aires) — direct from JFK, MIA, LAX, IAH; connections to USH (Ushuaia) and MDZ (Mendoza) Key Properties: Explora Patagonia (Torres del Paine), Awasi Patagonia, Palacio Duhau Park Hyatt (Buenos Aires)
02
Chile — Atacama, Patagonia & the Wine Valleys
Most Diverse Desert + Fjords Stargazing
San Pedro de Atacama · Torres del Paine · Santiago · Colchagua Valley · Easter Island
Chile is the most geographically extreme country in the world — 4,300 kilometers long and averaging 177 kilometers wide, spanning climates from the driest desert on earth in the north to the world's longest glacier system in the south, with a Mediterranean wine region, a Polynesian outlier island (Easter Island / Rapa Nui), and the shared Patagonian wilderness with Argentina in between. No other country contains this much landscape variation within its borders, and the Chilean travel experience reflects that variety in ways that most first-time visitors don't anticipate.

The Atacama Desert at San Pedro de Atacama is the region's most compelling singular experience. At 2,400 meters altitude in the driest non-polar desert on earth, the sky is clear enough on most nights that the Milky Way is bright enough to cast shadows, and the concentration of luxury lodges — Explora, Tierra Atacama, Nayara Alto Atacama — that have built their programming around the landscape (geyser walks at dawn, flamingo lagoons by afternoon, salt flat sunset, telescope-equipped stargazing after dinner) represents a specific type of destination travel that has few equivalents anywhere in the world. Chilean Patagonia, sharing Torres del Paine with its Argentine counterpart, is equally extraordinary; the approach from Puerto Natales by land, when the towers first become visible above the horizon, is one of the great landscape arrivals anywhere.
Atacama: Year-round; June – September (austral winter) clearest skies for stargazing Patagonia Best: November – March (austral summer; full trail access) Wine Harvest: March – April (Colchagua and Maipo Valleys) Gateway: SCL (Santiago) — direct from JFK, MIA, LAX, IAH; connections to CCP (Calama/Atacama) and PUQ (Punta Arenas) Key Properties: Explora Atacama (San Pedro), Tierra Atacama, Awasi Atacama, explora Patagonia (shared with Argentina)
03
Peru — Machu Picchu, the Sacred Valley & Lima
Inca Heritage Best Food City High Altitude
Lima · Cusco · Sacred Valley · Machu Picchu · Lake Titicaca · Amazon Lodge
Peru delivers two travel experiences of international reference quality in one country: the Inca archaeological circuit and Lima's food scene. They are different enough in character that most travelers who do both come back describing them as separate trips that happened to share a flight. Machu Picchu is genuinely extraordinary despite the management challenges of its popularity — the citadel at dawn, when the clouds are still in the valley below the terraces and the Inca stonework catches the first light, occupies a visual and spatial register that no photograph accurately captures. The correct approach is through the Sacred Valley: three nights at a lodge in the valley to acclimatize to altitude, then Aguas Calientes by train, then the citadel at first entry time (6am), then a private guide for three hours before the day crowds arrive.

Lima has become, by the assessment of critics who follow the global restaurant scene, one of the most important food cities in the world. The cuisine that Gastón Acurio and a subsequent generation of Peruvian chefs have built on the country's biodiversity — the 3,000 varieties of potato, the 650 varieties of native fruit, the ceviche culture that has been refined over four centuries of Pacific coast cooking — is not a single restaurant but an entire culinary ecosystem that exists within walking distance of the Miraflores and Barranco neighborhoods. Central, Maido, and Kjolle are three of the fifty best restaurants in the world according to various ranking bodies; all three are in Lima; none of them requires more planning context than a reservation.
Inca Trail Best: May – October (dry season; trail open; clearest views) Inca Trail Closure: February (maintenance); December – April (rainy season; trail muddy but operational) Altitude: Cusco at 3,400m — allow 2 full days to acclimatize before strenuous activity Gateway: LIM (Lima) — direct from JFK, MIA, LAX, IAH, IAD, ORD; connections to CUZ (Cusco) Key Properties: Belmond Sanctuary Lodge (Aguas Calientes), Explora Valle Sagrado, Inkaterra Machu Picchu Pueblo Hotel
04
The Galápagos Islands (Ecuador)
Nowhere Else Wildlife Expedition
Santa Cruz · Isabela · Fernandina · Española · Genovesa · Seymour Norte
The Galápagos Islands are the most significant wildlife destination outside Africa — and the most genuinely different, because the encounter dynamic is unlike anything else on earth. The wildlife here has no evolutionary history of mammalian predators. There are no land-based predators in the Galápagos, and over millions of years of isolation, the animals have developed no fear response to large moving things approaching at close range. A blue-footed booby will stand at the two-meter minimum visitor distance and observe you with frank curiosity. A marine iguana will not move. A sea lion will swim directly at you underwater, turn six inches from your mask, and swim away. The wildlife encounters are not the result of guides knowing where to find the animals — they are the result of the animals having no reason to leave when a human arrives. This is the only place on the planet where that is true for virtually every species.

The correct way to experience the Galápagos is by small-ship expedition cruise that moves between islands overnight and lands at visitor sites in the early morning before the larger vessels. Vessels carrying 16–20 passengers access the same sites as the larger ships but with smaller groups, shorter landing queues, and the ability to linger at sites until the panga (landing boat) calls them back. The itinerary of any given cruise is the same series of islands on a rotation managed by the Galápagos National Park; the quality of the experience is determined almost entirely by the vessel, the naturalist guides on board, and the group size. Darwin's finches, giant tortoises, flightless cormorants, waved albatrosses, Galápagos penguins — the species list is extraordinary and the encounter quality is consistent.
Cool Dry Season: June – December (clearer water; better diving; penguins active; whale sharks) Warm Wet Season: January – May (calmer seas; baby animals; sea turtle nesting; green landscapes) Gateway: UIO (Quito) or GYE (Guayaquil) to GPS (Galápagos/Baltra) — connections from MIA, JFK, IAH Key Vessels: Silver Origin (Silversea), Ecoventura, Aqua Mare — all 16–20 passenger capacity
05
Colombia — Cartagena, the Coffee Region & Medellín
Transformation Colonial City Coffee
Cartagena · Medellín · Salento · Coffee Triangle · Bogotá · Lost City Trek
Colombia is the most significant transformation story in South American travel. The country that spent two decades defined in the international imagination by a period of its history has become, in the years since, one of the most interesting travel destinations in the hemisphere — and the traveler who applies the old mental model to the current reality will miss a country that is worth considerable attention. Medellín was, in 1991, the most dangerous city in the world by murder rate. It is now a city with a cable car urban transport network that has connected previously isolated hillside neighborhoods to the city center, a Botero sculpture collection donated by the artist himself to a public plaza, a botanical garden, and a food and nightlife scene that has arrived without significant international notice. The gap between reputation and reality is nowhere wider in South America.

Cartagena's walled colonial city is one of the finest pieces of Spanish colonial urban design in the Americas — the pastel townhouses behind iron-balconied facades, the bougainvillea that falls over the walls of the converted-mansion hotels, the evening sea wall walk where the entire city seems to circulate at the same hour, the Plaza de la Trinidad in the Getsemaní neighborhood where the restaurants spill onto the streets after dark. The Coffee Triangle (Zona Cafetera) — Salento, Filandia, the coffee haciendas around Manizales — is the landscape from which the world's most celebrated single-origin coffee comes, and the road between the haciendas, with the wax palms rising from green valleys below, is among the most beautiful driving routes in South America.
Cartagena Best: December – March and July – August (driest; lowest humidity) Coffee Region: Year-round; harvest October – February (main crop) and April – June (mitaca crop) Medellín: Year-round (spring-like climate year-round; "City of Eternal Spring") Gateway: BOG (Bogotá) direct from MIA, JFK, IAH, ORD, LAX; CTG (Cartagena) and MDE (Medellín) from MIA Key Properties: Casa San Agustín (Cartagena), Hotel Quadrifolio (Cartagena), Casa Entonces (Coffee Region)
06
Brazil — Rio, the Pantanal & the Amazon
Jaguars Rainforest Rio Geography
Rio de Janeiro · Pantanal · Amazon · Fernando de Noronha · Iguazú · São Paulo
Brazil contains three travel experiences that each belong in a different category from the others. Rio de Janeiro's urban geography — Sugarloaf rising from the water, Corcovado and the Christ above the city, the curve of Ipanema beach framed by the Dois Irmãos peaks — is among the finest city settings in the world and requires no qualification or context. The city asks more of its visitors than most — the logistics are more complex, the awareness required is higher — and it returns more: the view from the top of Pão de Açúcar at sunset, with the city spread across the bays below and the mountains behind, is a sight that makes the preparation worthwhile without debate.

The Pantanal, the world's largest tropical wetland (a floodplain the size of France), is the best accessible wildlife destination in South America for sheer encounter density. In the dry season (July–October), the receding water concentrates the wildlife at permanent lagoons with a reliability that produces jaguar sightings on most full-day river expeditions — not guaranteed, but more consistent than almost any other big cat destination in the world. The Amazon's luxury lodge sector, anchored by properties like Cristalino Lodge in the southern Amazon and Anavilhanas Jungle Lodge near Manaus, has built an infrastructure that delivers the rainforest ecosystem — the canoeing through flooded forest, the night walks, the river dolphins, the bird lists that exceed 600 species per lodge — without the logistical compromise that characterized Amazon travel for decades.
Pantanal Jaguars: July – October (dry season; animals concentrate at water; highest sighting rates) Amazon Low Water: June – November (more wildlife visible; walking access; river beaches) Rio Best: April – June and August – October (cooler, drier; avoid Carnival crowds Dec–Mar if not attending) Gateway: GRU (São Paulo) or GIG (Rio) — direct from JFK, MIA, LAX, IAH, ORD, IAD; connections to CGB (Cuiabá/Pantanal) and MAO (Manaus) Key Properties: Caiman Ecological Refuge (Pantanal), Cristalino Lodge (Amazon), Santa Teresa Hotel (Rio)
Timing
When to Go — the Split Seasonal Logic
Nov – Mar
Southern Summer
Patagonia's primary window — the austral summer when trails are fully accessible, glacier calving is active, and the long days (18+ hours in January) make the most of the landscape. Mendoza wine harvest in March–April. Buenos Aires at its most vibrant September–November. The Iguazú Falls are at maximum flow December–March. Book Explora and Awasi Patagonia 9–12 months ahead for December–February.
Patagonia Peak
May – Oct
Dry Season
The primary window for Peru's Inca Trail (dry, clear, accessible), Galápagos diving (cooler water, better visibility, penguins active), Pantanal jaguars (dry season concentrates animals at water), and the Amazon low-water season (most wildlife access). The Atacama's austral winter (June–September) delivers the clearest skies and best stargazing of the year. Most destinations in this window can be combined efficiently within a single itinerary.
Wildlife & Hiking
Mar – May
Harvest & Shoulder
Mendoza's vendimia (grape harvest festival) in March is the wine region at its most alive. Patagonia's autumn — April and early May — brings fall colors to the lenga beech forests around Fitz Roy and Torres del Paine that photographers travel specifically for. The Inca Trail opens after February maintenance closure. Colombia and Cartagena are in a transitional period with generally good weather. Shoulder-season rates apply across most South American properties.
Year-Round
Lima & Colombia
Lima's overcast garúa season (May–November) affects the coast but not the restaurants; the city functions year-round and the food scene has no seasonal variation. Medellín has one of the most consistent climates in the world — the "City of Eternal Spring" designation is accurate; temperatures average 22–24°C every month. Cartagena's best weather is December–March, but the city is operational and worthwhile in most months. The Galápagos has two distinct seasons but no bad one.
Properties Worth Knowing
Eight Properties That Earn Their Rates
Not a comprehensive list — these are the specific lodges, hotels, and expedition vessels across South America that consistently deliver what they promise, from the salt flats of the Atacama to the jaguar rivers of the Pantanal to a colonial mansion in Cartagena's walled city.
Explora Patagonia
Wilderness Lodge
Torres del Paine · Magallanes Region · Chile
Fifty rooms in a building designed by Germán del Sol on the shore of Lago Pehoé, inside Torres del Paine National Park, with the granite towers visible from the dining room. Explora's model — all-inclusive with daily guided excursions led by their own trail guides, no activity à la carte — was designed around a specific philosophy: that Patagonia requires the expertise of people who know the terrain intimately to deliver properly. The guides at Explora have typically been working these trails for years and calibrate the day's excursion to the weather window rather than a fixed schedule. It is the most organizationally sophisticated wilderness lodge in South America and has been since it opened in 1993.
Awasi Atacama
Desert Camp
San Pedro de Atacama · Atacama Desert · Chile
Twelve private villas in the Atacama desert outside San Pedro de Atacama, each with its own vehicle and dedicated guide — meaning the day's program is entirely private, departure times are yours, and the excursions (geysers at 4,500m altitude, flamingo lagoons, salt flat photography, Valle de la Luna) are paced to your group rather than a shared tour schedule. The Atacama at altitude produces cold nights regardless of season; the open-air tubs in the private courtyards are most useful in winter, when the temperature contrast between the still-warm water and the clear desert air makes the stargazing above the tub something guests consistently describe as the best night of the trip. Awasi's guide quality is the highest in the region.
Belmond Sanctuary Lodge
Ruins Gateway
Aguas Calientes · Machu Picchu · Peru
The only hotel adjacent to the Machu Picchu citadel — a 31-room property built into the cloud forest at the entrance to the site, which means that guests can enter the citadel at opening time (6am) before the first buses from Aguas Calientes arrive and can return after the last bus has left. The morning window — two hours with the site at minimal population, the clouds still in the valley below the agricultural terraces, the light changing from blue to gold across the Intihuatana stone — is what the Belmond rates buy. Everything else at the property is secondary to that access. Book the rooms facing the garden and the cloud forest, which are quieter than those facing the bus terminal.
Silver Origin
Expedition Vessel
Galápagos Islands · Ecuador
A 100-guest expedition ship — large enough to carry a submarine and multiple zodiacs, small enough to access the same sites as the 16-passenger boutique vessels — operated by Silversea with all-inclusive expedition programming and a Relais & Châteaux-level food and service product. The Galápagos National Park regulates vessel itineraries on a rotation system; every vessel visits the same core sites on a rolling schedule, so the choice of ship is purely about the on-board product rather than destination access. Silver Origin's naturalist guides average 15+ years in the Galápagos and hold the national park's highest guide certification. The submarine provides underwater access to sites that snorkeling cannot reach, including a hammerhead aggregation point at Darwin Island that Silver Origin visits on the longer itineraries.
Palacio Duhau Park Hyatt
City Palace
Recoleta · Buenos Aires · Argentina
165 rooms across two connected buildings in the Recoleta neighborhood — a restored 1934 French-style palace and a modern tower built into the hillside below it, connected by a garden and underground walkway. The wine bar, built into a brick-vaulted cellar below the garden, holds 1,800 labels across Argentina's wine regions and is the finest hotel wine program in Buenos Aires. The Recoleta Cemetery — where Evita Perón is buried alongside the country's former presidents, in a walled city of mausoleums that architecture critics take seriously — is a five-minute walk. The Alvear Art Hotel and the Four Seasons are Buenos Aires' other reference properties; the Duhau wins on wine and the garden.
Caiman Ecological Refuge
Jaguar Reserve
Miranda · Mato Grosso do Sul · Brazil · Pantanal
A 53,000-hectare working cattle ranch in the southern Pantanal that has been running wildlife conservation programs since the 1980s, with three intimate lodges (Baiazinha, Cordilheira, and Sede) positioned across the property to provide access to different ecosystems — river, gallery forest, flooded campo. The Onçafari jaguar research program, based at Caiman, has habituated several jaguar individuals to vehicle presence over years of non-invasive observation; the result is that jaguar encounters at Caiman are calmer, longer, and at closer range than at any other Pantanal operation. The encounters are not guaranteed but the habituation work means that when the jaguars are found — and they are found on most full-day expeditions in the dry season — the experience is qualitatively different from most big cat encounters anywhere.
Casa San Agustín
Walled City
Old City · Cartagena · Colombia
Thirty rooms in three restored colonial mansions inside Cartagena's walled city, connected by a courtyard and a rooftop pool that looks over the terracotta tiles of the old city toward the sea wall and the Caribbean. The property was assembled from buildings that have been occupied continuously since the 16th century; the original stone walls, the internal courtyards, and the iron-detailed windows were preserved in a restoration that took several years and resulted in the finest boutique hotel in Cartagena. The location — on a quiet street off the Plaza de los Coches, inside the walls — means the evening city (the squares, the restaurants, the street musicians) is walkable from the front door. The rooftop at sunset, when the old city below turns gold and the sea breeze arrives from the Caribbean, is the specific experience this hotel was built around.
Cristalino Lodge
Amazon Lodge
Alta Floresta · Mato Grosso · Brazil · Southern Amazon
A private 11,000-hectare reserve in the southern Amazon — one of the most biodiverse privately held parcels in Brazil — with a 30-room lodge on the Cristalino River that has been operating since 1999 and has built a naturalist guide team with some of the deepest species knowledge of any Amazon operation. The bird list for the reserve exceeds 620 species. The canopy tower, accessible by ladder and suspended 40 meters above the forest floor, provides a 360-degree view of the rainforest canopy at sunrise that most Amazon lodges cannot offer — the morning reveals parrots, macaws, monkeys, and the specific scale of intact Amazon rainforest that no ground-level experience communicates. The lodge is serious about conservation research and partners with multiple Brazilian universities; the guides' knowledge of the forest reflects this investment.
